lead: Don't spend all your energy on "what I'm bad at"; also look at how you contribute most easily.
when: When you're choosing what to study, assigning roles, or have long seen only the ways you fall short of others, this is well worth using.
body:
Strengths-based thinking encourages you to notice the abilities you use well again and again, the ones other people genuinely benefit from. Some people are good at explaining complicated things, some are good at catching what's been missed, and some can bring strangers together. Putting those abilities into the right tasks and continuing to practice them often builds confidence and results more easily than staring at your weak spots forever.

A strengths-based approach emphasizes identifying, developing, and using the abilities and resources a person or system already has in order to improve performance and growth, while managing the weaknesses that must be addressed to reach a goal.

But a strength isn't a label like "that's just how I'm made." It depends on real performance, the conditions where it works, and feedback, and it still needs basic skills underneath it. If you're good at coming up with ideas, you still need to explain and follow through. If you're good with details, you also need to keep small issues from holding up all your progress.
example:
On your team, you always feel behind the others because you're slow at writing long reports. But whenever a discussion gets messy, people come to you to lay out the problem clearly and sketch how things connect. Looking back at those moments, you may realize that what you're good at is sorting things out and explaining them on the spot.

You could talk it through first, record it, and then turn it into a report. You could also team up with someone who's good at writing things up, while still practicing basic writing. It's not that you never write again. You've found an entry point that suits you better, and you're using the abilities you already have to help cover what you lack.
extra: You're not good at speaking off the cuff in a big group, but you can write very clear questions ahead of time. You could send a discussion outline first and then gradually practice speaking up. Finding a way that works is an easier place to start than forcing yourself to become someone else first.
steps: Look back at three tasks you did well and got specific feedback on, and find what they have in common.
Ask under what conditions this ability works best, instead of just giving yourself a name for a strength.
Actively seek out suitable tasks, use tools and teamwork to support your weak spots, and build up the basics you need.
caution: "I'm not good at it" can't be an excuse to never learn or to hand every hassle to someone else. Strengths can also be overused; for example, being thorough can turn into endless nitpicking, so adjust to the situation.
exercise: Ask a friend who knows you well: "What's something you'd especially want to come to me for help with? Can you give a specific example?" Then compare the answer with your own experience.
brief: Using strengths while managing necessary weaknesses: one stick figure uses a long pole they're skilled with to cross a gap in a task, while a teammate fills in a small step for a weakness that must be covered. On the left, five ability bars of different lengths, with the tall bar standing out as support for the goal and the lowest, riskiest bar reinforced.
sources: Gallup · How to Develop and Use Your Strengths
